lesson.title: Reading Colors: How Flame Tests Reveal an Element's Identity
lesson.summary: A flame test uses the characteristic color of light emitted when a heated metal's electrons fall back to lower energy levels to quickly identify which metal ion is present.
lesson.body:
A flame test is one of the fastest confirmatory tests available in qualitative analysis: touch a clean wire loop, dipped in a solution or moistened salt, to the edge of a flame, and the color the flame turns can identify which metal ion is present, often in seconds and without any precipitate at all. It works because the heat of the flame temporarily excites electrons in the metal atom or ion to a higher energy level. As those electrons fall back down to their original, lower energy state, they release the extra energy as a photon of light, and because each element has its own distinct set of allowed energy levels, that photon has a wavelength, and therefore a color, that is characteristic of the element.

This is exactly the mechanism behind emission spectra, just compressed into a single visible color instead of a full spectrum of separated lines. A flame test is really a crude, whole eye version of emission spectroscopy: instead of passing the light through a prism to see every individual wavelength an element emits, you are looking at the overall color your eye perceives from the strongest emission lines blended together.

The colors themselves are consistent and worth knowing by heart, because they show up constantly in both qualitative analysis and real applications like fireworks chemistry. Sodium burns a strong yellow-orange, so strong that even a trace contaminant of sodium can mask other colors. Potassium gives a pale lilac or violet. Copper burns blue-green. Lithium gives a crimson red flame, calcium an orange-red, strontium a red, and barium a green. Lithium and strontium are both often described as red, but an experienced observer can usually tell them apart: lithium's flame reads as a deeper, more crimson red, while strontium's is a brighter scarlet red. In a mixed unknown, sodium's intense yellow-orange is the biggest troublemaker: it can overpower a weaker signal from another metal, which is why a chemist checking for potassium, for instance, will sometimes view the flame through blue cobalt glass to filter out sodium's interference.

The energy carried by the emitted photon can be calculated directly from its wavelength using E = hc / lambda, where h is Planck's constant, 6.626 x 10^-34 J·s, and c is the speed of light, 3.00 x 10^8 m/s. Sodium's characteristic yellow-orange light has a wavelength of about 589 nm, or 589 x 10^-9 m. The photon energy is:

E = (6.626 x 10^-34 J·s x 3.00 x 10^8 m/s) / (589 x 10^-9 m) = 3.37 x 10^-19 J

Converting to electron volts by dividing by 1.602 x 10^-19 J/eV gives about 2.11 eV, which matches the well known energy gap for sodium's outer electron transition. That single number explains the whole test: the color you see is a direct, visible readout of the energy gap between two electron orbitals inside the atom.

Because the color depends on the identity of the element and almost nothing else, a flame test is a genuinely independent check, exactly the kind of second line of evidence that qualitative analysis calls for when a precipitate alone cannot pin down which cation is present.
